name: Finding Adjacent Numbers in Ascending Order in a Sequence of Numbers
description: Construct a program that checks whether a sequence of non-zero numbers, entered one at a time, contains adjacent numbers in ascending order. Numbers are said to be in ascending order when they are arranged from the smallest to the largest number. For example, 5, 9, 13, 17 and 21 are arranged in ascending order.\nNote that you need to think what value should the program use to indicate the end of the input.
code:
#Step 1: Read the first number that the user enters
text = input("Enter a number: ")
num = float(text)
#Step 2: Read the rest of the numbers that the user enters and check for adjacent numbers in ascending order
while num != 0 :
    previous = num
    text = input("Enter a number: ")
    num = float(text)     
    if num != 0 and num > previous :
        print(previous,"and", num, "are in ascending order.")

comments.content: We need to read and process the input value that the user enters. To read the input value from the user, we need to use the input() function. This statement prompts the user to enter the first number. The value that will be stored in variable text is a string.
We need to convert the input text to its float representation because the number could have a decimal point. For this purpose, we use the conversion function float().
Note that this can only be done if user input could be translated into a valid floating-point value.

We need to repeat receiving the number from the user as long as the user enters a non-zero number. Therefore, we need to use a loop structure. Since we don't know ahead of time how many times the loop will be repeated, we need to use a while loop. The condition in the while loop tests whether the body of the loop should be repeated, so it should test whether the input number is not equal to the value that indicates the end of the input. In this program, we designate 0 to indicate the end of the input because it is outside the normal range of numbers that the user will enter.
The body of the while loop is repeated as long as the user enters a number that is different from 0. The loop terminates when the loop condition evaluates to False, that is when the user enters 0.
We store the number that the user entered in a variable called previous because we want to later compare it with the next number that user will enter to check if they are in ascending order.

We need to read and process the next number that the user enters. To read the input value from the user, we need to use the input() function. This statement prompts the user to enter the next number. The value that will be stored in variable text is a string.
We need to convert the input text to its float representation because the number could have a decimal point. For this purpose, we use the conversion function float().
Note that this can only be done if user input could be translated into a valid floating-point value.

We need to test if the number that the user entered is different from 0 because 0 indicates the end of the input and we need to skip it. We also need to test whether the number that the user entered and its previous number are in ascending order. To determine if the two number are in ascending order we need to check if the value of variable num is greater than the value of variable previous.
If the number that the user entered is different from zero and greater than its previous number, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
Note that the and operator yields the result True if both conditions are True.

This statement prints to the default standard output stream, the two adjacent integers that are in ascending order.
The printed text shows the arguments of the print function separated by the default delimiter (i.e., single space character) and followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
